rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi treats 20:74–76 as a divine insertion: their afterlife register suits God’s majesty, differs from the surrounding speech, and recalls an earlier insertion at 20:53–59.
rows.anchor: This verse and the two succeeding ones are from God.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A wrongdoer here is someone disobedient to God who has not repented.
rows.anchor: The word “wrongdoer” in the translation refers to a person who is disobedient to God and did not have the courtesy to repent.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase about neither dying nor living depicts punishment from which death offers no relief and no escape exists.
rows.anchor: Death can alleviate the greatest of punishments.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The succeeding group contrasts with the damned: only faith accompanied by righteous deeds has weight; faith without deeds is fruitless, like an infertile tree.
rows.anchor: Faith that is without righteous deeds has no significance.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The promised reward is for people who purify themselves ideologically, practically, and morally, following the Qur’an’s guidance about pitfalls and human concessions.
rows.anchor: Only they will be eligible to it who will try to purify themselves

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rejecting the Qur’an’s guidance in pursuit of religious purification leads to extremism.
rows.anchor: Rejection of any of these things will lead to extremism in religion.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi rejects theologians’ wishful claim that deeds are unimportant: the Qur’an does not promise Paradise on that basis, whose key remains with God; Jewish false hopes are discussed in al-Baqarah.
rows.anchor: those who out of their own desire have reduced the importance of deeds, whether they belong or our classical theologians or those of modern times

rows.speaker: al-Zamakhsharī
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī explains the idiom as meaning “to make way.”
rows.anchor: as has been explained by al-Zamakhshar ī

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi sees a subtle allusion to Moses’ staff in the expression for making a path, since the staff creates the path through the sea.
rows.anchor: to the staff of Moses (sws) because it had a role in “making way.”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verb’s object is omitted through parallel construction; the full sense is that Moses faces neither capture by Pharaoh nor drowning.
rows.anchor: the object of the verb

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The account suppresses the years of confrontation: Pharaoh repeatedly promised release after calamities were lifted, then renewed oppression, while Moses continued delivering God’s message.
rows.anchor: he would sweet-talk Moses (sws) to pray to ward off this calamity

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After the truth was fully conveyed, God ordered Moses to migrate with the believers; initially Moses had sought permission to take Israel to a nearby desert for three days.
rows.anchor: the truth had been fully delivered to them

rows.speaker: Ḥam īd al-Dīn Far āhī
rows.claim: Farāhī’s reported view is that Moses wanted to take the people to Makkah for the rites of animal sacrifice.
rows.anchor: In the opinion of my mentor, Ḥam īd al-Dīn Far āhī, he wanted to take them to Makkah to carry out the rituals of animal sacrifice.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “My servants” means all who accepted faith regardless of lineage: most were Israelites, with a smaller group of Egyptian converts.
rows.anchor: to those who had accepted faith

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Indications place some converts among the Egyptians, including magicians who accepted faith from both Egypt and Israel; the Qur’an also mentions a righteous believer in Pharaoh’s family.
rows.anchor: Concomitant indications show that the magicians who had accepted faith belonged to the Egyptians and to the Israelites.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sea is identified as the southern gulf of the Red Sea; Moses was to strike its water with his staff to form a dry route, a display of God-given authority.
rows.anchor: strike the sea water with his staff, thereby creating a dry path for them.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The definite article on “the sea” indicates that God had specified the destination to Moses.
rows.anchor: a clear evidence where God had instructed Moses (sws) to go.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an mentions a righteous believer from Pharaoh’s household.
rows.anchor: a righteous believer who belonged to the Pharaoh’s family.

rows.speaker: Torah
rows.claim: Exodus recounts the sea being driven back by a strong east wind, leaving dry ground and walls of water for Israel to cross.
rows.anchor: this miracle was the result of a strong eastern wind. The gulf was divided into chunks of water separated by dry land.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Arabic expression for what covered Pharaoh’s army conveys that the horror of the event exceeds verbal description.
rows.anchor: horrific nature of something is beyond expression.

rows.speaker: Torah
rows.claim: Exodus says Pharaoh reversed his decision after Israel left, pursued them with his army, and lost the entire force when the sea returned; Islahi cites this as corroboration.
rows.anchor: the book of Exodus, this incident is recorded in the following words:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse regrets Pharaoh’s failure as a leader: rulers must guide their people like shepherds, and the worst shepherd sacrifices the flock to ego.
rows.anchor: the responsibility of every leader and ruler to correctly guide their nation.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After rescue, God recalls His favors to Israel to remind them of the duties those favors impose and the fate of ingratitude; the parallel appears with slight wording changes in 2:46–57.
rows.anchor: reminded the Israelites of His great favours

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The promise at the blessed side of Mount Ṭūr was God’s promise through Moses to give the Israelites the Torah; Moses had been called at this site when returning from Madyan.
rows.anchor: called them to this blessed side of the mount Ṭūr.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The manna and quails and Israel’s response to them were explained under 2:57.
rows.anchor: have been explained under verse 57

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The gifts obligate Israel to eat pure provisions and avoid rebellion; prophets and the Torah reminded them, and abundance must not make them arrogant like Pharaoh.
rows.anchor: mention the obligation they owe to these favours.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rebellion invites God’s wrath and destruction, lowering a person from honor to humiliation; Israel had just witnessed Pharaoh’s fate.
rows.anchor: from a state of honour

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The closing verse gives a path to deliverance: repent, believe, do good deeds, and remain guided.
rows.anchor: The last verse mentions the path of deliverance

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The preposition after “hasten” signals an elided verb that collocates with it (taḍmīn); Islahi’s translation reflects that grammatical construction.
rows.anchor: the suppressed verb collocates with the preposition.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God summoned Moses to the place where he had received prophethood so he could receive the Torah; Moses was assigned thirty days and left Aaron in charge, but arrived early from eagerness to meet God.
rows.anchor: God fixed a time period

rows.speaker: Torah
rows.claim: Exodus describes Moses going up the mountain with Joshua and leaving Aaron and Hur to handle disputes, but gives no thirty-day period or account of Moses’ haste.
rows.anchor: The Torah mentions this but does not state any time period

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In 7:142 the appointment is thirty nights plus ten, and Moses tells Aaron to reform the people and avoid the corrupters; Islahi says God added ten days to train Moses against haste.
rows.anchor: in order to train and instruct him for showing haste

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses’ haste arose from zeal to please God, not a base motive, yet it became a trial: the calf-worshippers exploited his absence and Aaron could not control them.
rows.anchor: was the result of his zeal and his passion to earn God’s pleasure.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Israelites had shown an emotional tendency to idolatry: after crossing the sea they had asked Moses to make an idol like those worshipped by neighboring peoples.
rows.anchor: they demanded from him to make an idol for them

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Prophets’ mistakes do not arise from low desires; they may exceed limits through zeal for truth and pleasing God, and God corrects them because they model truth for others.
rows.anchor: this attitude in itself is not something bad

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The episode teaches Muḥammad that patient waiting for God’s decree is proper in struggles for His cause, since even pious haste can become a pitfall.
rows.anchor: showing patience and waiting for God’s decree is the right behaviour for such struggles in His cause

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God’s established practice tests both individuals and nations to distinguish right from wrong; Israel failed this test when Sāmirī led them astray.
rows.anchor: it failed the test

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an names Sāmirī as the instigator and clears Aaron, whom Torah narrators had blamed for the mischief.
rows.anchor: it has exposed the name of the actual originator

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sāmirī’s ethnicity is immaterial; Islahi declines that debate and describes him as a cunning hypocrite who entered Moses’ followers with evil motives and used mystifying tricks.
rows.anchor: I would not like to enter into this debate.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses’ early departure and the extra ten days gave Sāmirī an opportunity to gather Israelites already drawn to idolatry, solicit their jewelry, and promise a guiding deity while Moses was absent.
rows.anchor: afforded with opportune time to play his tricks.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An adept Egyptian idol-maker fashioned a calf from the jewelry that bellowed when wind passed through it, then attributed the sound to magic and deceived the people.
rows.anchor: when the wind would pass through it, a certain sound came out of it.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sāmirī fooled the masses by attributing the calf’s sound to magic.
rows.anchor: He regarded this sound, as will become evident later, to be a consequence of his magic.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Aaron tried to stop the mischief, but the people were too taken by Moses’ authority; fearing danger to his life and communal division, he waited for Moses to return.
rows.anchor: he felt that if he now takes any step

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses returned in anger and grief: anger at wrongdoers and Aaron’s apparent failure, and grief that the nation worshipped a calf while Moses fetched its guidance.
rows.anchor: He returned to his people in great anger and grief.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses grieved at the nation’s wretchedness, worshipping a calf while he had gone to fetch God’s guidance.
rows.anchor: wretchedness of his nation

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The broken promise refers to Moses’ instruction that the elders wait for his return with the law and follow Aaron meanwhile.
rows.anchor: He had told them to follow the directives of Aaron (sws) during this time.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The elders say they did not break their promise willingly: they returned the entrusted jewelry when its owners demanded it, leaving Sāmirī and the deceived people responsible.
rows.anchor: They said that they did not have any role in whatever happened

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word milk means will or power; the elders claim events exceeded their control despite their efforts to keep the promise.
rows.anchor: The word ﻣَﻠۡﻚ means “will and power.”

rows.speaker: Torah
rows.claim: Torah accounts conflict over jewelry ownership: Exodus 35 indicates Israelite ownership, while another account says Israel borrowed it from Egyptians.
rows.anchor: The Torah contains conflicting statements

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi rejects the borrowed-from-Egyptians account as implausible and morally untenable; he prefers that the jewelry belonged to the Israelites, supported by 7:148.
rows.anchor: This second account appears to be illogical.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi holds that the jewelry belonged to Israelites, citing 7:148 as corroboration.
rows.anchor: the jewellery belonged to the Israelites.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The chiefs’ language conveys the weight of the entrusted burden they carried before casting it down; Islahi infers that Moses accepted their excuse.
rows.anchor: allude to heaviness of the burden these chiefs felt.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verb can mean casting down or throwing up; the chiefs describe discarding the burden, while alqā can also mean performing a trick, as in 20:65.
rows.anchor: cast down or to throw up.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verb alqā has broad senses, including placing something down, casting dice, or showing a trick; the chiefs blame Sāmirī for the deception.
rows.anchor: it also means to throw dice and show a trick or stunt.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because their helplessness seemed evident, Moses apparently accepted the elders’ excuse.
rows.anchor: it seems that Moses (sws) accepted their excuse.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The chiefs held Sāmirī entirely responsible for the mischief.
rows.anchor: The chiefs held S āmir ī to be entirely responsible for this mischief.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Khuwwār means a calf’s bellow: Sāmirī’s calf was a body from which the sound of a bull came.
rows.anchor: signifies the bellowing of the calf.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Egyptian idol-making was highly developed; a skilled maker could construct a calf that sounded when wind passed through it.
rows.anchor: In those times, this art was at its zenith in Egypt.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sāmirī deceived the people by claiming Gabriel’s horse-hoof dust caused the calf to sound.
rows.anchor: the dust created by the hooves of Gabriel’s horse in this statue

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi compares Sāmirī’s tricks with even greater modern magicians and asks how hard it would be to fool simple Israelites.
rows.anchor: could it have been difficult for him to deceive a simple nation as the Israelites.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Propaganda said the calf was the deity of the people and Moses, who had supposedly forgotten it; most Israelites were drawn into the mischief.
rows.anchor: The result of this propaganda was that a vast majority of the Israelites

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A deity is a person’s greatest need, so an inert calf that cannot answer, harm, or benefit is unfit for worship.
rows.anchor: What need will such a lame deity fulfil that has made them worship it?

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Aaron disavowed the calf; the Qur’an firmly clears him despite Torah’s attribution of the origin to him.
rows.anchor: the Qur’ ān has vehemently negated it.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word “already” shows Aaron warned the people immediately when the calf mischief emerged.
rows.anchor: as soon as this mischief surfaced

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The people ignored Aaron; although some later recognized their folly, as al-A‘rāf shows, they persisted in calf-worship until Moses returned.
rows.anchor: deceived by Satan

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses’ directive to Aaron was to lead the people, watch the wrongdoers, and prevent mischief; his question seeks Aaron’s reason, since Moses knew he would not disobey deliberately.
rows.anchor: would not deliberately disobey him

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Against grammarians who call the second lā redundant, Islahi says it emphasizes the verb, a familiar Arabic construction also found in Urdu.
rows.anchor: to emphasize the verb

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses’ grasping Aaron’s beard and head reflects both religious honor and natural brotherly love; prophets tolerate worldly matters but do not compromise in religion, especially with those close to them.
rows.anchor: in religious affairs, they do not compromise in any way.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Worldly-minded people show the reverse pattern: cautious in worldly affairs, they lack sensitivity when close relatives err in religion.
rows.anchor: in religious affairs, they do not have any sensitivity

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Aaron says he tried to stop the people, but Sāmirī’s spell swayed most of them and Aaron feared for his life; separating with his followers risked division and bloodshed, so he waited for Moses’ return and authority.
rows.anchor: The first option would have resulted in divisions among people and bloodshed.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After questioning those who might be responsible and identifying Sāmirī as the source, Moses asks him what happened.
rows.anchor: After asking all those who could be responsible for the mischief

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sāmirī claims a vision of Gabriel and says he took dust from the messenger’s footprint and put it in the calf; Islahi reads this as a self-serving excuse and admission that his own soul deceived him.
rows.anchor: He said that he had a vision and saw something which others did not

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sāmirī recasts his action as an unintentional misconception, claiming he mistook his soul’s prompting for a vision, though he knew his bluff would not easily succeed with Moses.
rows.anchor: he regarded the deceptive prompting of his soul to be a vision and hence committed this crime.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses’ command to go away means “get lost”; Sāmirī’s sentence that he will keep saying “do not touch me” signifies lasting exclusion from social contact.
rows.anchor: here means “to go and get lost.”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi says Sāmirī himself will warn others not to touch him and will be unable to touch anyone, remaining ostracized for life.
rows.anchor: call out to people that he was impure and thus should not be touched

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The punishment resembles the Mosaic law of cutting an impure person off from the community; Islahi supports this with Leviticus 7.
rows.anchor: there exists a punishment to sever someone from the community.
